studies.title: With Reason And A Term
studies.meaning: Two claims sit side by side before any argument begins. The scripture comes down from God, named here by power and wisdom together. Then creation is said to have been made with truth and for a set term, which denies two things at once: that the universe is purposeless, and that it is permanent. The closing clause does not argue with those who refuse. It reports their posture. They are turning away from a warning already delivered, which makes the difficulty attention rather than evidence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later stretch of the mission there, when opposition had hardened from curiosity into settled refusal. The surah opens the way its six immediate predecessors open, and shares their concerns: where the Book comes from, the emptiness of what is worshipped alongside God, and the ruin of earlier peoples. No specific occasion is reported for these opening ayat. The commentators read them as the surah stating its own subject before it begins.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun, not a verb, so the phrase names the act rather than narrating it. The form carries a sense of gradual descent, which suits a book delivered across two decades.
Literally a named limit. The second word means it has been specified, not merely that one exists, which makes the end of the world a fixed appointment rather than an eventual wearing out.
From a root meaning to present one's side. The image is a body angled away rather than a mind that has weighed and rejected, so refusal is described as a bodily habit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything the first listeners owned had a term on it. A lease on a well ran out. A truce between tribes held for a named number of years. Dates were bought before harvest against a stated date, and a debt fell due on a day both parties could count to. Arabic had a precise vocabulary for such deadlines. Saying that the heavens and the earth carry one placed the sky in a category they already knew how to think about.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the last of seven consecutive surahs, numbers forty to forty-six, that open with the same two disconnected letters. All seven were revealed in Mecca, and the tradition of reciters has long treated them as a family. The group is the longest unbroken run of surahs in the Quran sharing an identical opening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage joins revelation and cosmology in one breath, and the join is the argument. A universe made with purpose and given a deadline is a universe in which a warning makes sense; a universe that simply is would make any message beside the point. The two divine names chosen carry the same pairing. Power without wisdom would be arbitrary, and wisdom without power could not act on what it saw.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle in the surah immediately before this one, and adds that each soul is repaid.
Denies that the heavens and the earth were made in play, using the negative form this passage uses.
Puts the appointed term inside a call to reflect on oneself, rather than in an argument with opponents.

studies.applyIt: Pick one object near you that you expect to outlast you, a building or a hill on the horizon. Give it a number of years. You will be wrong, and that is the point of the exercise. The passage says the sky itself has a date on it. Holding that thought for thirty seconds tends to rearrange what feels urgent.

studies.title: Show Me What They Made
studies.meaning: The challenge is framed as a request for evidence, and it names the two kinds that would count. Either produce something in the world these objects have made, a patch of earth or a share in the heavens, or produce a text: an earlier scripture, or any surviving trace of transmitted knowledge. The demand is not that opponents feel differently. It is that they show their working. The last clause makes truthfulness the standard, so the argument is about honesty as much as about proof.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The shrine at the centre of the city held images associated with a long inherited practice, and its authority came from age and custom rather than from any book. The surah presses exactly there. Its opening ayat had claimed a scripture sent down from God; this one asks the other side for the equivalent. No particular occasion is reported. The commentators treat it as part of the surah's opening argument about origins.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a track left behind. It covers a fragment of transmitted learning handed down from earlier generations, so the challenge accepts oral tradition as evidence and still asks for it.
The ordinary commercial word for a stake in a venture. Used of the heavens it makes the claim measurable: name the portion these objects own, the way a partner names his.
A command to make visible, not to explain. It asks for something that can be pointed at, which is a harder demand than the argument the opponents were prepared to have.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on evidence of a particular kind. A trader's reputation rested on witnesses who had seen a transaction. Genealogists carried lineages in memory and could be challenged on a name. Poets were judged in public, line against line, before crowds who knew the older verses. A city that assessed claims this way could recognise the shape of this request even when it did not like where it pointed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered as a trace of knowledge occurs only here in the whole Quran, and its exact reading was discussed early: some reciters read the word as a single trace, others with a form suggesting selection or a chosen report. All the readings keep the sense of something inherited from earlier generations rather than freshly reasoned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the burden of proof on inherited practice rather than on the new message, which reverses the usual direction of religious argument. It also sets out what would count against a claim, in the world or in a text, and by doing so treats belief as something answerable to evidence. Truthfulness appears at the end as a moral quality bound to an intellectual one: saying what you cannot show is placed among the failures of character.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same double demand almost word for word: what have they created, and where is their book.
Asks opponents for a clear authority and tells them to bring their scripture if they are truthful.
Applies the same standard to any claimant: produce your proof, whoever you are.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you hold firmly and ask yourself where you first got it. Not whether it is right, only where it came from. Most convictions turn out to have arrived from somebody rather than from evidence, and noticing that is not the same as abandoning them. It is the habit this ayah is asking for, turned on yourself first.

studies.title: A Call That Never Arrives
studies.meaning: The failure described is not that the call is refused. It is that nothing at the other end is listening. Two separate defects are named: no answer will come, and the ones addressed are unaware that anyone is addressing them. The time limit given is not a short one. The silence runs to the Day of Resurrection, so no future moment will correct it. Then the scene shifts to that day, when the objects of all that devotion become opponents and disown the worship they were given.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage follows a demand for evidence and moves from argument to consequence, which is the surah's habit. Pilgrimage to the Meccan shrine was a fixed part of the regional year, and appeals were made there for rain, for safe caravans, for children. No specific occasion is reported. The commentators read the passage against that ordinary practice rather than against any single incident.

keyTerms.note: A form that means to answer a request, not merely to reply. The word is used elsewhere of God answering prayer, so its denial here is precisely targeted at what the caller wanted.

Heedlessness rather than refusal. It describes something that never registered at all, which is a colder verdict than rejection: the prayers were not heard and then declined, but simply never arrived.
The plural of a word used for open hostility between tribes. On that day the relationship inverts completely, and what was petitioned for help stands on the other side of the case.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A petition in that world went through a patron. A man without a strong clan sought protection from a chief, and the arrangement was public: the protector announced it, and everyone knew whose name stood behind whom. Its value depended entirely on the patron acknowledging you when the moment came. The nightmare was arriving at a crisis and finding that the man whose name you had been using did not know who you were.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the same verb for calling on God and for calling on anything else, and the difference is carried by what follows, not by the word itself. In this passage the identical verb appears in one ayah for the act and its result. The neutrality of the verb is why the argument here has to be about the answer rather than the asking.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures worship by whether it lands, which is an unusual test. Sincerity is not questioned; the callers are assumed to mean it. What fails is the receiving end. That separates devotion from its object and refuses to let the intensity of feeling validate its direction. The scene of disowning on the last day extends the point: attachments formed in this life do not bind the thing attached to.

crossReferences.why: Says the same objects do not hear the call, and would not respond even if they did.
Gives the direct contrast: God is near and answers the call of the one who calls.
Shows the same reversal, where what was taken as support becomes a denier and an opponent.

studies.applyIt: Notice, once today, where you actually turn first when something goes wrong. Not what you would say if asked, but the reflex: a person, a screen, a plan, a name. The passage is not asking you to feel guilty about it. It is asking you to see the direction of the turn, because you cannot redirect a habit you have never watched.

studies.title: Clear Called Obvious Magic
studies.meaning: The sentence is built so that two words collide. The signs are recited plain and clear; the verdict returned is that this is obviously magic. The same adjective sits on both sides. Whatever quality made the recitation unmistakable is the quality being cited as proof of sorcery, which is the point: the effect was admitted and only its source was disputed. Note also what is not said. No counter-argument is offered, only a label, and the label conveniently ends the conversation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. By this stage the recitation was being heard in the streets and at the shrine, and its effect on listeners was a practical problem for the city's leadership. Classical sources describe attempts to discourage visiting pilgrims from listening. Calling it sorcery was one of a set of charges, alongside poetry and soothsaying, that placed the words in a known category and so removed the obligation to weigh them.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning not merely clear but clarifying, something that makes other things plain. Applied to the recited signs it claims they carry their own evidence rather than needing external support.
In seventh-century usage it covered anything that produced an effect by hidden means, including persuasion so powerful it seemed uncanny. The charge concedes the power while relocating its cause.
The same root as the word used a moment earlier for the clarity of the signs. Placing it on the accusation makes the ayah's irony structural rather than a matter of tone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had recognised specialists in powerful speech. Soothsayers spoke in short rhymed bursts and were consulted about lost camels and disputed paternity. Poets were believed by many to draw on a companion spirit, and a satire from a famous one could damage a tribe's standing for a generation. A man who heard extraordinary words had ready categories for them, and reaching for one of those categories was the ordinary response, not a desperate one.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase translated here as obvious magic appears nine times across the Quran, and in almost every case it is spoken by opponents about a revelation or a miracle, including by Pharaoh's court about Moses. The repetition is part of the argument: the same verdict is shown being returned in different centuries by different people.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates rejection after recognition rather than before it. What is described is not a failure to perceive but a decision about how to file what was perceived, which makes the moral weight fall on the naming rather than on the hearing. It also sets a limit on what evidence can accomplish. Clarity is granted by the ayah itself, and clarity turns out not to be sufficient, because a name can be found for anything.

crossReferences.why: Records the identical verdict, and adds that they returned it the moment truth reached them.
Shows Pharaoh's people saying the same words about the signs given to Moses.
Preserves the reasoning behind the charge: this is transmitted magic, this is human speech.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you reach for a category before you have finished listening. The word might be naive, or political, or overrated. Notice that the label arrived faster than any thought, and let the sentence finish anyway. You can still reject it afterwards. The passage is about the gap between hearing and filing, and that gap is where attention lives.

studies.title: Thirty Months And A Prayer
studies.meaning: The instruction is brief; the reason takes over the sentence. The mother's labour is named twice with the same word, in pregnancy and in delivery, before any duty is spelled out. Then the ayah jumps forward to a man of forty and gives his words rather than his deeds: a prayer to be enabled to be grateful, to act well, and to have his own children set right. Gratitude to parents and to God are folded into one request.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah that alternates between argument with Meccan leaders and portraits of individual response. Reports attaching this ayah to a particular companion circulate in the commentaries, but they differ over who is meant and the classical writers generally read the wording as describing any believer who reaches middle age. The contrast is with the son in the ayat just after, who answers his parents with contempt.

keyTerms.note: The same word covers what is repugnant and what is carried against inclination. Repeating it for bearing and for delivering refuses to soften either, and it is stated as fact rather than as a claim on the child.

A rare imperative asking to be held to something, used elsewhere in the Quran only by Solomon. The man does not ask for gratitude to appear; he asks to be gathered and restrained until he produces it.
A plural-shaped noun for the peak of a person's powers, used of Joseph and of Moses at the point where each was given judgement. Here it is paired with an exact number of years, which is unusual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Childbirth in seventh-century Arabia was survived rather than managed. Women delivered at home with the help of relatives and a midwife, and a family could name the babies it had lost as readily as the ones it kept. Nursing ran close to two years, and a mother's milk was a bond strong enough to create kinship in Arab custom. Thirty months was a measurable stretch of a woman's life, not a figure of speech.
studies.didYouKnow: Read beside two other passages, this one yields a piece of arithmetic the classical scholars noticed early: thirty months for carrying and weaning together, and two full years given elsewhere for weaning alone, leaves six months for the pregnancy. The deduction is one of the oldest examples of reading two separated ayat as a single statement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Kindness to parents is grounded in something already done rather than in authority, so the claim is presented as a debt of fact. The prayer at forty then turns the whole ayah forward: the mature believer does not ask to repay his parents but to be made capable of gratitude, which means the capacity itself is treated as a gift. Repentance is placed at the end, in a life that has gone well.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same enjoinment with a different image, weakness upon weakness, and supplies the two years this passage assumes.
Turns to the moment the relation reverses, when a parent grows old and the child is asked for gentleness in speech.
Contains the only other use of the rare verb in this prayer, on Solomon's lips after he overhears an ant.

studies.applyIt: If a parent of yours is alive, ask them one factual question this week about the year you were born: where they lived, what the work was, what they were afraid of. Do not turn it into an apology or a thank-you. The ayah begins with information, not sentiment, and most people find they are missing more of it than they expected.
